newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian liberals start gvt no-confidence procedure.
newsitem.headline: Russian liberals start gvt no-confidence procedure.

text.p: Russia's liberal Yabloko bloc started collecting signatures on Friday for a vote of no-confidence in the government because of a severe budget crisis.

Yabloko's leader, economist Grigory Yavlinsky, told a news conference that 38 signatures had been collected almost immediately in the State Duma, the lower house of parliament, and 52 more were needed to put the issue on the agenda.

The motion by what is a relatively small force in the Duma appears unlikely to be approved because the communist-led chamber rarely supports the liberals' proposals, but Yavlinksy's attack comes at a hard time for the cabinet.
Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin's government is trying to push through a plan to cut spending by one fifth to tackle the budget crisis, a move fiercely opposed by deputies.
Government officials say revenues were 30 to 50 percent short of budgeted levels in the first quarter. April's tax collection also lagged by about 20 percent.
Chernomyrdin is due to report on first quarter spending and revenue results on May 21. First Deputy Prime Minister Anatoly Chubais will present the plan to cut spending, or sequestration.
The Duma will vote on sequestration two days after the ministers' reports.
Yavlinsky said cutting spending should not be an option.

"With the budget crisis in full swing the government should have proposed a law recognising the 1997 budget as inoperative and started drafting the 1998 budget immediately, using 1996 budget levels for the rest of this year," Yavlinsky said.
Such measures were urgent and indispensable, he said.
He added that under no circumstances would his group support a plan to print some additional 300 trillion roubles ($52 billion) in cash which has been proposed by communist deputies.
The central bank has already said it will not support the plan which is says would trigger hyperinflation.

Duma speaker Gennady Seleznyov, a communist, said on Thursday the Duma would not approve the sequestration plans in their current form but that it may be ready for compromise to reduce the size of the proposed spending cuts.
The Duma's budget committee said it would recommend that the chamber reject the spending cuts. The Duma on Wednesday ordered the Audit Chamber to check the government's sequestration plan.
Yavlinsky criticised the government for failing to present any plans for increasing revenues.

"This means that the government is unable to fulfil its functions. On this basis, Yabloko has decided to sequester the cabinet," Yavlinksy said. "The main problem of the government is that it has a full no-confidence vote from the people."

He said the sequestration plans meant government economic policy was unrealistic. "It also means that this year Russia will have no economic policy that can lead to stabilisation or economic growth," he said.
Russian government officials say the Kremlin can find other ways to cut spending if parliament does not approve the plan, but that sequestration is a better solution.

The Duma, elected in December 1995, has tried before to pass a no-confidence motion in the government but has either fallen short of the number of signatures required to start the procedure or lacked support when the motion was put to the vote.
If such a motion were approved, President Boris Yeltsin would face a choice between disbanding the government or the parliament. ($ = 5761 Russian Roubles)
